I am 70 this year, and I have farmed these 20 mu in Quzhou for half a century. I finished high school, which was not common when I was young, so I read whatever planting guides I can get, and I talk to the seed dealer and the old technicians who come through the village. But 50 years of working this land teaches you more than any paper.

My land is split into two parts. Sixteen mu are my good, flat fields where I run the wheat-maize double crop. That is the backbone of my farm. The other four mu are sandier, closer to the old riverbed, and I plant cotton there. Cotton handles that soil better, and it gives my family cash in the autumn when grain prices dip.

For winter wheat, I plant an improved variety at about 15 kg per mu. I sow around October 10th, just like last year — the soil was warm enough and the seedlings wintered well. My base dressing is 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, which gives me 7.5 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Then at green-up in March, I top-dress with 20 kg of urea per mu, another 9 kg of nitrogen. That brings my total nitrogen to about 16 kg per mu. I used to go as high as 20 kg, but I watched the test plots in Wangzhuang over the last five years, and I saw that 16 kg was enough if you put it on at jointing when the roots can grab it. I would rather spend the yuan on the second dressing than waste it in the autumn. I irrigate four times: before sowing, once in the winter if the ground is dry, once at jointing in late March, and once at flowering in late April. My well water is fresh, not salty like in some eastern villages, so I do not worry about salt buildup.

For summer maize, I switch to no-tillage. After wheat harvest in early June, I have about ten days before the summer drought hits. I plant a hybrid, Zhengdan 958, at 3 kg per mu. I put down 30 kg of compound fertilizer at sowing, and at the big trumpet stage in mid-July, I side-dress with 25 kg of urea per mu. Total nitrogen is about 15 kg per mu. Some neighbors still dump it all at sowing, but splitting it gives me fuller ears. I irrigate twice — at jointing and at flowering — because July and August usually bring some rain, and pumping costs electricity.

My four mu of cotton I handle carefully. I rotary till in mid-April and plant then. Cotton is hungry early but then needs you to hold back water once the bolls open. I use about 12 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between base and first flowering. Phosphorus and potassium I keep at 5 kg each per mu — any more and the sandy soil grows too many leaves and not enough bolls. I spray four times: first for aphids in June, then bollworms in July, then mites in August, and one more cleanup before harvest. I hire a drone for the grain crops, but for cotton I walk the sprayer myself because the drone cannot hit the underside of the leaves where the mites hide.

I expect my wheat to yield about 550 kg per mu, the maize about 600 kg per mu, and the cotton about 220 kg of seed cotton per mu. These are honest numbers — I have hit them before. The input bill runs about 1,800 yuan per mu for wheat-maize and about 1,200 yuan for cotton. With grain prices where they are and cotton holding steady, I should clear enough to cover family costs and help with my grandson’s schooling.
